authoring_notes: Authored for the api-call branch learning schema and the existing Domain 3 question bundle. Uses CompTIA's official objective IDs 3.1-3.4 as skill IDs because the bullet examples under each objective are not separately numbered. Content is definition-first, keeps tables mobile-friendly at no more than three columns, teaches the exact concept IDs used by Domain 3 questions, and treats architecture choices as scenario-dependent tradeoffs rather than universal rules. Supporting claims were checked against NIST and IETF references where appropriate.

prompts.label: TRADEOFFS
prompts.placeholder: Which architecture question is being asked?

cells.question: Can service continue through failure, and recover quickly?
What do redundancy, operations, licenses, and staffing cost?
Does the design meet latency or time-sensitive needs?
Can capacity grow without redesigning everything?
How safely and consistently can changes be released?
Which financial or operational risk is shifted by contract, insurance, or outsourcing?
How hard is it to rebuild or restore the service?

reveal.text: There is rarely one architecture that maximizes security, cost, speed, and availability at the same time. Identify the scenario's priority first, then choose the design whose tradeoff matches it.

nodes.title: Active, passive, inline, and monitor-mode devices

cells.meaning: Can take action that changes or blocks traffic.
cells.risk: Can prevent attacks, but incorrect action can disrupt traffic.

modules.title: Protect data by type, state, and location

prompts.label: DATA TYPE
prompts.placeholder: What kind of data is it?

cells.meaning: Handling is governed by an applicable law or regulation.
cells.example: Data with legally mandated protection or retention.

cells.meaning: Confidential business information that derives value from remaining secret.
Creations or proprietary knowledge with legal or business value.
cells.example: Source code, designs, patents, copyrighted works.

cells.meaning: Information created or retained for legal matters.
Information about money, transactions, accounts, or financial operations.
A person can directly interpret the content.
cells.example: Plain text or a visible report.

cells.meaning: A specialized parser, decoder, or application is needed to interpret it.

reveal.text: Data type describes what the information is or why it matters. It is different from a classification label, which is an organization's handling label.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: CLASSIFICATION
prompts.placeholder: What does a classification label do?

reveal.text: A data classification label communicates required handling based on sensitivity, business impact, or policy. Security+, for example, lists sensitive, confidential, public, restricted, private, and critical.
Do not assume every organization ranks these labels in the same order. Use the policy and scenario to determine what each label means and which controls it requires.

nodes.title: Data at rest, in transit, and in use

prompts.label: THREE STATES
prompts.placeholder: Where is the data right now?

cells.meaning: Stored and not actively moving between systems.
Moving across a network or communication channel.
cells.example: API request, file transfer, VPN traffic.

cells.meaning: Actively processed or accessed by a running system.
cells.example: Data in application memory while being processed.

reveal.text: Match the protection to the state: storage controls and encryption for data at rest, protected protocols for data in transit, and strong access/process isolation for data in use.

glossary.definition: The legal authority whose laws or regulations apply to a person, organization, activity, or location.

nodes.title: Encryption and hashing for data protection

columns.title: Encryption
items: Transforms data using a cryptographic key so unauthorized parties cannot read it.
Primary goal here: confidentiality.

columns.title: Hashing
items: Produces a fixed-size digest from data.
Useful for detecting changes or comparing values; it does not hide the original data by itself.

reveal.text: If the requirement says 'keep the contents secret,' hashing alone is not enough. If the requirement says 'detect whether this value changed,' a cryptographic hash may be appropriate.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

prompts.label: COMPARE
prompts.placeholder: How is the sensitive value changed?

cells.idea: Hide or replace part or all of a displayed value.
cells.clue: Show only the last four digits.

cells.idea: Replace a sensitive value with a non-sensitive token; the original value is kept separately or recoverable through the token system.
cells.clue: Applications use a surrogate value instead of the real identifier.

cells.idea: Make information or code harder to understand.
cells.clue: Discourage easy interpretation; not a substitute for strong encryption when secrecy is required.

reveal.text: Masking changes what a viewer sees. Tokenization substitutes a different value for the sensitive one. Obfuscation makes interpretation harder, but does not automatically provide cryptographic confidentiality.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

columns.title: Segmentation
items: Separates systems, datasets, or paths so compromise in one area does not automatically expose another.
Think: isolate where data can be reached from.

columns.title: Permission restrictions
items: Limit which identities or processes can read, change, delete, or administer data.
Think: limit who can do what.

reveal.text: Protect sensitive data with both reachability limits and authorization limits. 'Can this system reach the data?' and 'Is this identity allowed to use it?' are separate questions.

nodes.title: Hot, warm, and cold recovery sites

prompts.label: RECOVERY SITE
prompts.placeholder: How ready is the alternate site?

cells.readiness: Systems, connectivity, and data are prepared for rapid operation.
cells.tradeoff: Fast recovery; highest ongoing cost and maintenance.

cells.readiness: Some systems and connectivity are prepared; additional restore or configuration is needed.
cells.tradeoff: Middle ground for cost and recovery time.

cells.readiness: Facility and basic resources exist, but systems/data need significant setup or restoration.

reveal.text: When a scenario demands the shortest recovery time and accepts higher cost, a hot site is the usual fit. When cost matters more than recovery speed, warm or cold options may fit better.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

columns.title: Geographic dispersion
items: Places redundant resources far enough apart to reduce shared location disasters and utility failures.

columns.title: Platform diversity
items: Uses different platforms or technologies to reduce dependence on one shared implementation or failure mode.

reveal.text: Diversity can reduce correlated failures, but it adds operational complexity, training needs, integration work, and more configurations to secure.

glossary.definition: A failure that affects multiple redundant components because they share the same underlying dependency, location, provider, or defect.

prompts.label: MULTI-CLOUD
prompts.placeholder: Does two providers automatically mean resilience?

reveal.text: A multi-cloud design uses services from more than one cloud provider. It can reduce dependence on one provider, but only provides failover value when data, identity, networking, operations, and recovery are actually designed to work across providers.

Continuity of operations focuses on keeping essential functions available or restoring them during disruption. Architecture supports this with alternate capacity, documented recovery paths, trained people, and tested procedures.

prompts.label: THREE CAPACITIES
prompts.placeholder: What must be available during normal operation and recovery?

cells.question: Are enough trained responders, operators, and decision-makers available?
Are compute, storage, software, licenses, and services sufficient?
Are network, facilities, power, and supporting resources sufficient?

reveal.text: Recovery capacity is not only CPU and storage. A technically redundant system can still fail operationally if trained people, network capacity, power, licenses, or facilities are missing.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0

nodes.title: Tabletop, failover, simulation, and parallel testing

cells.action: Participants discuss a scenario and walk through decisions without switching production.
Service is transferred to the alternate system or site to verify it can take over.
A realistic event is exercised in a controlled way without necessarily disrupting production.
cells.clue: Practice the response under simulated conditions.

cells.action: Primary and alternate processing run at the same time so results/capability can be compared.

reveal.text: A plan you never test is only an assumption. Use low-risk exercises to find procedural gaps, then progressively test technical failover and recovery where business risk allows.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 — Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems

glossary.definition: The point when production service or workload is switched from one environment to another.

nodes.title: Backup strategy: location, frequency, encryption, snapshots

cells.why: Offsite copies reduce the chance that one site disaster destroys production and every backup.
More frequent recoverable copies reduce the amount of recent work that may be lost.
Backups can contain the same sensitive data as production and require confidentiality protection.
Point-in-time copies can speed recovery, but their failure domain and retention must be understood.

reveal.text: Do not treat a snapshot as automatically equivalent to an independent offsite backup. Ask where the copy lives, whether the same failure can destroy it, whether it is protected, and whether restoration has been tested.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-209 — Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure

columns.title: Replication
items: Copies data or system state to another location or system.
Supports availability and recovery, often with low delay.

columns.title: Journaling
items: Records changes or transactions so state can be reconstructed or replayed.
Useful for point-in-time recovery and understanding the sequence of changes.

reveal.text: Replication is not a replacement for protected backups. A deletion, corruption, or bad change may also replicate unless separate recovery points are retained.

source_refs.title: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 Exam Objectives v6.0
NIST SP 800-209 — Security Guidelines for Storage Infrastructure

columns.title: UPS
items: Battery-backed power starts immediately when utility power is interrupted.
Bridges short outages or the startup time of longer-duration power.

columns.title: Generator
items: Produces power for longer outages once started and supplied with fuel.
Supports extended operation but normally takes time to start.

reveal.text: Think 'UPS now, generator longer.' A resilient facility also plans fuel, maintenance, testing, safe shutdown, and the power needs of network and cooling systems.
